physical_harm: No injury was caused to the complainant
key_evidence_accepted: The CFSL Report proves that the cartridge recovered from the office of the complainant was fired from the service pistol recovered from the appellant. The Medico-Legal Report and testimony of the doctor corroborate the ocular versions of the complainant, his clerk, and his steno that the appellant was in an inebriated condition when he entered the residential office of the complainant. Both the complainant and PW-4 have categorically testified that after consuming water, the appellant pulled out his pistol and aimed it at the complainant.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the main witnesses as credible, noting that their testimonies corroborated each other and were supported by forensic evidence. The court found the defense's version of events to be 'a patch of lies and figment of imagination' and rejected it entirely.
bail_history: Appellant is on bail, his bail bonds are discharged
trial_duration: Dates of offence: 10th July 1999; Trial judgment: 25th July 2006; High Court decision: 19th May 2010; Supreme Court decision: 26th November 2021
legal_representation: Counsel for the accused: Jasbir Singh Malik, Ms. Usha Nandini, V, Advs.; Counsel for the State: Manpreet Singh Doabia, Anil Kumar, Sudarshan Singh Rawat, Advs.
investigation_status: FIR registered, charge sheet filed, trial completed
appeal_history: Trial court: Convicted and sentenced to 3 years; High Court: Sustained conviction and sentence; Supreme Court: Partly allowed the appeal, set aside conviction under Section 27 of the Arms Act, reduced sentence under Section 307 IPC to period already undergone
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the appellant, in an inebriated condition, pulled out his service pistol and aimed it at the complainant, thereby attempting to murder him. The CFSL Report confirmed that the cartridge recovered from the complainant's office was fired from the appellant's service pistol. The prosecution maintained that the appellant's conduct was sufficient to constitute an offense under Section 307 IPC.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the appellant's version of events was more plausible, suggesting that the complainant had accidentally fired the weapon. They claimed that the complainant had fabricated the incident to avoid criminal liability and that the appellant had no motive or intent to kill.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the doctrine of proportionality in sentencing, emphasizing that the severity of the sentence should be proportionate to the gravity of the offense, considering mitigating factors such as the absence of injury, the appellant's clean record, and the passage of time.
precedent_relied_upon: State of Madhya Pradesh vs. Saleem @ Chamaru & Anr. (2005) 5 SCC 554; Shivaji Genu Mohite v. State of Maharashtra (1973) 3 SCC 219; Bipin Kumar Mondal vs. State of West Bengal (2010) 12 SCC 91; State of M.P. vs. Kashiram & Ors. (2009) 4 SCC 26; Jage Ram & Ors. v. State of Haryana (2015) 11 SCC 366; State of M.P. vs. Kanha @ Om Prakash (2019) 3 SCC 605
sentencing_rationale: The sentence was reduced to the period already undergone due to mitigating factors such as the absence of injury, the appellant's clean record before and after the incident, and the passage of a long time since the offense.
judicial_mitigating_factors: The appellant's clean record, the absence of injury, the passage of a long time since the incident, and his unblemished service record with sixteen good citations.
other_sentence_order: The conviction under Section 27 of the Arms Act was set aside, and the sentence under Section 307 IPC was reduced to the period already undergone. The appellant's bail bonds were discharged.
